**Hans Otto Roth** (29 April 1890 – 1 April 1953) was a [Transylvanian Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvanian_Saxon "Transylvanian Saxon") politician and lawyer. Roth was best known for his unsuccessful attempts to counter the rise of the radical [Nazism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazism "Nazism") favored within the [German Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Party_(Romania) "German Party (Romania)") and within the German ethnic group in Transylvania.

Born in [Sighișoara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sighi%C8%99oara "Sighișoara"), Roth studied law at various universities around Europe before graduating with a doctorate from the [ELTE Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELTE_Faculty_of_Law "ELTE Faculty of Law") in 1913. In 1918, Roth joined the Saxon Central Committee to support the [unification of Transylvania with Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Transylvania_with_Romania "Union of Transylvania with Romania"). In 1919, he won a seat in the [Chamber of Deputies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_of_Deputies_(Romania) "Chamber of Deputies (Romania)") representing the [German Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Party_(Romania) "German Party (Romania)"), and by 1922, he replaced [Rudolf Brandsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rudolf_Brandsch&action=edit&redlink=1 "Rudolf Brandsch (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Brandsch "de:Rudolf Brandsch")) as Parliamentary Chairman of the party. His time in parliament saw him focus on the issues of denominational schools and cooperation between the Germans and Hungarians before he retired in 1938. During his time in parliament, he was also briefly Chairman of the Association of German Minorities from 1931 to 1934, where he at first advocated for [pan-Germanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Germanism "Pan-Germanism"). He met [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") in June 1933, which altered some of Roth's views, although many Jews in Transylvania still felt betrayed by Roth.

In the following years, Roth became increasingly anti-Nazi with the advent of the "renewal movement". Roth's views were generally considered [Christian liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_liberalism "Christian liberalism"), which put him in opposition to many of the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party")'s views. He was approached many times to be a minister in various Romanian cabinets, but declined because of the fact that the [Iron Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Guard "Iron Guard") all had places in these cabinets. In 1943, this led to a climax between [Andreas Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Schmidt_(politician) "Andreas Schmidt (politician)") and Roth, and Roth was expelled from the party. He kept working at the time as regional church curator of the [Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession in Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Church_of_the_Augsburg_Confession_in_Romania "Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession in Romania"), a position he had held since 1932. His various attempts to stop the self-Nazification of the church led to failures. After the [1944 Romanian coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Romanian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "1944 Romanian coup d'état"), Roth asked Saxons to remain loyal to the Romanian state and wrote numerous memorandums to the Romanian government asking them not to judge his people too harshly. Roth was first arrested in August 1948, which triggered a wave of alarm, although he was eventually released. He was re-arrested in 1952 and held in the Ghencea concentration camp, where he died.

Early life and education
------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Hans Otto Roth was born on 29 April 1890 in [Sighișoara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sighi%C8%99oara "Sighișoara") on the street Kleingasse 1 (now Strada Tache Ionescu), which was then part of [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-jahr-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-str-3) He was the sixth and youngest child of lawyer and city judge of Sighișoara Karl Roth (1846–1901) and Louise Roth (née Hausenblaß, 1855–1915) and was the grandson through his maternal side of a factory owner.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bi2-5) He attended elementary school in Sighișoara where he graduated in 1900, and then attended the local Protestant high school in Sighișoara until 1908 where he was a part of the student self-government called Coetus Chlamydatorum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4) From 1908 to 1912, he studied law at the universities of Budapest, Vienna, Berlin, and Zurich.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-tradition-6)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4) In April 1913, he received his [doctorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorate "Doctorate") in law from the [ELTE Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELTE_Faculty_of_Law "ELTE Faculty of Law") of the [University of Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Budapest "University of Budapest"), where he was also the president of the League of Transylvanian Saxon Students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-jahr-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bi2-5) Afterwards, from 1913 to 1915, he worked in the Budapest law firms of A. Teteleni and Karl Schmidt.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4)

At the start of World War One, Roth was initially deemed unfit for service, so he became deputy editor of the Transylvanian Saxon daily newspaper _Siebenbürgisch-Deutsches Tageblatt_, replacing Hermann Plattner, who had been drafted.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-weg-7) He worked under the leadership of Emil Neugeboren.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-weg-7) In January 1916, he was conscripted for military service in the [Austro-Hungarian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Army "Austro-Hungarian Army"), and he served as an auxiliary for Infantry Regiment No. 31 in [Brno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brno "Brno"), performing exclusively clerical duties.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-weg-7) He was briefly sent to [Semmering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semmering,_Austria "Semmering, Austria") during his time in the military to recover from apical [catarrh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catarrh "Catarrh") of the lungs.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-weg-7) In February 1917, he was released from military service due to illness.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4) Afterwards, from February 1917 to 1918, he was an editor for _Siebenbürgisch-Deutsches Tageblatt_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-jahr-2) In 1918, the [union of Transylvania with Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Transylvania_with_Romania "Union of Transylvania with Romania") occurred, which inspired Roth to become secretary of the Saxon Central Committee, where he supported the union and the accession of Saxons to Romania.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-museum-8) He was specifically chosen as secretary for aligning with the "Little Saxon" tradition, which advocated for legalism and integration into Romania, which had started to be prominent around 1900.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bi2-5) The tradition acknowledged the cultural value of [pan-Germanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Germanism "Pan-Germanism") but advocated keeping it separate from state politics, opposing efforts to implement it through political means such as territorial annexation, due to concerns about its legality.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bi2-5) He was elected over more politically experienced politicians like [Rudolf Brandsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rudolf_Brandsch&action=edit&redlink=1 "Rudolf Brandsch (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Brandsch "de:Rudolf Brandsch")), who advocated for a more radical pan-Germanic ideology, which the Little Saxons disagreed with as they thought merging into a greater German identity would dissolve the Saxon identity and erode their cultural heritage.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bi2-5)

In 1919, Roth was part of the Saxon delegation that handed the decision of the Saxon representatives to the government in [Mediaş](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media%C5%9F "Mediaş"), and afterward, the Saxon Central Committee announced the Transylvanian Saxons' decision to join the Kingdom of Romania.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-museum-8) Roth also wrote the Saxon People's Program during this time, which was adopted on 6 November 1919, and he was thus considered a key player in the integration of Saxons into Romania.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-9) He wrote the program after many Saxons complained about the reforms following the accession, and he also led a delegation of Saxon peasants to [Cluj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluj "Cluj") to present their complaints to the Directory Council.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-10)

[![Image 2: Man in a suit and tie looking directly at the camera, in a portrait-style shot](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Rudolf_Brandsch.jpg/250px-Rudolf_Brandsch.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rudolf_Brandsch.jpg)

Rudolf Brandsch (pictured here) and Roth were rivals in the German Party for most of Roth's career.

In the [1919 Romanian general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_Romanian_general_election "1919 Romanian general election"), Roth won a seat in the [Chamber of Deputies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_of_Deputies_(Romania) "Chamber of Deputies (Romania)") representing the [German Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Party_(Romania) "German Party (Romania)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-11) In a speech in October, the month before the elections, he stated his campaign consisted of renewing confidence in the national vitality of Saxons, recognizing that the rejection of Hungary was not a betrayal and was justified citing the "abandonment" of the minority, and affirming that the pledges of [King Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Ferdinand_I_of_Romania "King Ferdinand I of Romania") to follow the results of the [Great National Assembly of Alba Iulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_National_Assembly_of_Alba_Iulia "Great National Assembly of Alba Iulia") were honest.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-12)

In 1922, Roth replaced Rudolf Brandsch as leader of the Parliamentary Group of the German Party.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-13) Roth was generally believed to have been chosen to replace Brandsch because Brandsch favored the strengthening of German self-consciousness and did not want to seek compromises with the ruling [Romanian National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_National_Party "Romanian National Party"), while Roth saw the possibility of the German-Romanians rights being enforced by a compromise.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-par-14) At the time in 1922, Roth admitted that he did not see ripe cooperation at the moment, but thought it only "conceivable", as he acknowledged [Iuliu Maniu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iuliu_Maniu "Iuliu Maniu")'s position and said that the Romanian government was favorable to Saxons.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-par-14) He also stated that the Germans had a desire to contribute to Romania's development through what he called "constructive work" rather than political confontration.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-die-15) Roth's advocacy was ultimately successful as it led to a gain in seats for the party in the parliament and the government meeting some demands.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-kulturs-16)

Soon after, in December, Roth defined what the German Party wished at a conference: the unconditional recognition of the Romanian state of the Saxons, full political and parliamentary activity even in matters that did not concern the minority, and implementation of the people's political program.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-die-15) In parliament, Roth tried to secure the rights he thought were promised to Germans, including German-language schools, equal rights in the economy, preservation of assets of the [Transylvanian Saxon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvanian_Saxon_University "Transylvanian Saxon University"), and land ownership.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-17) In 1924, Roth made a repeated plea for [denominational schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_school "Religious school"), saying it was clearly enshrined in the 1919 Peace Treaty, and saying that Romania was "virtually confiscating" minority rights.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-speech-1) This eventually led to the [Private School Act of 1925](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Private_School_Act_of_1925&action=edit&redlink=1 "Private School Act of 1925 (page does not exist)"), which standardized the Saxon school system.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-speech-1) Roth characterized the legislation as a test of Romania's tolerance towards minorities.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-speech-1) That same year, with the growth of pro-[Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party") sentiments in Transylvania, Roth stated in an essay that fascism was "a setback of the national political movement" which had fought for the protection of self-determination for ethnic minorities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4)

[![Image 3: A portrait of a gentleman with neatly styled hair, wearing a suit and a striped tie](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Hans_Otto_Roth_1926.jpg/170px-Hans_Otto_Roth_1926.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hans_Otto_Roth_1926.jpg)

Roth in 1926.

[Alexandru Averescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_Averescu "Alexandru Averescu")'s 1925 [agrarian reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform "Land reform") led to famine among the German-Romanians, especially in [Bessarabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessarabia "Bessarabia").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4) The shipping agency [Cosulich Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosulich_Line "Cosulich Line") exploited the desperate German farmers by charging excessive fees for emigration to Brazil, which Roth condemned.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4) Roth, after visiting the emigrants, demanded an investigation into the line and heavily criticized the Romanian government for what he perceived as its failure in addressing that the line purposefully exploited and took away the belonging of the emigrants who wished to go to Brazil.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-bio-4)

In the autumn of 1921, the [Hungarian Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyar_Party_(Romania) "Magyar Party (Romania)") proposed a joint political approach, which Roth rejected as too early.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-par-14) By 1923, the two parties began to collaborate extensively to resist Education Minister [Constantin Angelescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Angelescu "Constantin Angelescu")]'s school decree (Nr. 100.008 and 100.090) as the regulations threatened their denominational schools.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-par-14) They formally met in February 1925 after the Hungarians reorganized at the German House of Representatives in Bucharest, where it was agreed there would be liaison officers instead of a straight [minority bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Minority_bloc&action=edit&redlink=1 "Minority bloc (page does not exist)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-par-14) In August 1925, Roth formally proposed joint political action between the two minority parties, but the cooperation fell apart in 1926 when Roth found out that the Hungarian Union had been secretly negotiating with the [National Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Liberal_Party_(Romania,_1875) "National Liberal Party (Romania, 1875)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-par-14) In 1927, a brief [Hungarian German Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_German_Bloc "Hungarian German Bloc") occurred, but it dissolved soon after.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-18)

Roth officially retired from parliament in 1938.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-19) One of his last actions in parliament was in January when he was received by King [Carol II of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_II_of_Romania "Carol II of Romania"), where they discussed the German ethnic groups in Romania.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-20) In 1939, he was made a [senator by right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senator_by_right "Senator by right") in the [Senate of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Romania "Senate of Romania"), which he was awarded because he had won a seat in parliament in ten elections in accordance with the [1923 Constitution of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Constitution_of_Romania "1923 Constitution of Romania").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-21)

### Association of German Minorities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Association of German Minorities")]

In 1931, Roth was appointed Chairman of the _Verband der deutschen Minderheiten in Europa_ ([Association of German Minorities in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_of_German_Minorities_in_Europe&action=edit&redlink=1 "Association of German Minorities in Europe (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verband_der_deutschen_Minderheiten_in_Europa "de:Verband der deutschen Minderheiten in Europa"))).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-kulturs-16) By this time, Frühmesser, his biographer, interpreted that Roth approved of a pan-Germanist policy that included [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Austrian_Republic "First Austrian Republic") because he expected it to have a positive impact on the Germans in Eastern Europe.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-at-22) His appointment as chairman was largely just a figurehead position, as the Reich wanted leadership that would not be portrayed in a radical National Socalist light and would not interfere in tthe Association's Berlin operations.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-verband-23)

In 1933, Roth led a large-scale parade in [Passau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passau "Passau"), where he said that Germans feel unimaginable pain due to conflicts.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-24) On 15 June 1933, in his capacity as chairman, Roth had a conversation with [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler"). In the meeting, Roth drew attention to the fact that the [anti-semitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-semitic "Anti-semitic") measures of the [German Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Reich "German Reich") could have a negative impact on the treatment of German minorities, although Hitler defended his moves and dismissed Roth's concerns.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-at-22) This caused Roth to start rejecting Hitler and Nazism. Three months later at the European Congress of Nationalities, Roth spoke about nations dissimilating, a nod to [Jewish Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Germans "Jewish Germans") being excluded.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-at-22) His views were inconsistant, as he still at first advocated for dissimilation, while at the same time saying no nation-state can be built on the annihilation of other people.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-at-22) This led to many [Jews in Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews_in_Romania "Jews in Romania") having an increasingly harsher stance against Roth, as they believed he no longer took any stance against the persecution of Jews.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-selb-25) He was replaced by [Kurt Graebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kurt_Graebe&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kurt Graebe (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Graebe "de:Kurt Graebe")) in 1934.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-verband-23)

### Rise of Nazism and World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Rise of Nazism and World War II")]

[![Image 4: Head shot of a man with a very short haircut, facing to his left](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Andreas_Schmidt_%28Volksgruppenf%C3%BChrer%29.PNG/250px-Andreas_Schmidt_%28Volksgruppenf%C3%BChrer%29.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andreas_Schmidt_(Volksgruppenf%C3%BChrer).PNG)

In 1943, the conflict between Andreas Schmidt (pictured here) and Roth intensified to where Schmidt removed Roth from the [Ethnic German Group of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Party_(Romania) "German Party (Romania)").

Upon the [National Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Party_(Romania) "National Socialist Party (Romania)")'s dissolution in 1934, many blamed Roth as an internal opponent to it by using the church's influence to overthrow the now-renamed German Party, the _Nationalsozialistische Erneuerungsbewegung der Deutschen in Rumänien_ (Movement of National Renewal of Romanian German; NEDR), along with spreading rumors in the _Kronstadter Zeitung_ newspaper against it.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-26) This was because Roth's views were generally considered [Christian liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_liberalism "Christian liberalism"), which put him in opposition to many of the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party")'s views.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-pars-27) He was then attacked by a [Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi "Nazi")-affiliated newspaper, who said that Roth's leadership was "rotting internally" without a backbone and accused him of disrespecting the Germans who died in the [Battle of Langemarck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Ypres "First Battle of Ypres") and calling them "stupid boys".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-28) Roth also received criticism in 1936 from Nazi-aligned members within the Transylvanian Saxon community, who accused him of dissolving [Völkisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%B6lkisch_movement "Völkisch movement") organizations to replace them with loyal commissioners, deliberately harming the other main Transylvanian Saxon party at the time called the [German People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_People%27s_Party_(Romania) "German People's Party (Romania)"), and that his banking policies led to loss of land.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-nz-29) He had long been an opponent of the increasingly popular [Nazi renewal movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nazi_renewal_movement&action=edit&redlink=1 "Nazi renewal movement (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erneuerungsbewegung_(Zeit_des_Nationalsozialismus) "de:Erneuerungsbewegung (Zeit des Nationalsozialismus)")) under [Fritz Fabritius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Fabritius "Fritz Fabritius"), with [Andreas Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Schmidt_(politician) "Andreas Schmidt (politician)") calling him a divider of the movement.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) However, Roth encouraged his circle to join the [National Renaissance Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Renaissance_Front "National Renaissance Front"), a surrogate party for the Nazis, in 1939 due to tactical reasons, although he deliberately missed the deadline for admissions to be a member himself.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30)

On 4 July 1940, Roth was appointed Minister of State for Minorities in the [Gigurtu cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigurtu_cabinet "Gigurtu cabinet").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-appt-31) His appointment was generally believed to be because King Carol II wanted to preserve the territorial possessions of Greater Romania, which he though Germany would enforce after seeing the successes of the [Wehrmacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht "Wehrmacht") on the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_II) "Western Front (World War II)") in 1940.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-appt-31) Roth declined the appointment as he did not want to share the responsibility for the awarding of Northern Transylvania to Hungary with the [Second Vienna Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Vienna_Award "Second Vienna Award"), he decried the appointment of [Iron Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Guard "Iron Guard") members in the cabinet, and he feared that Nazis would "set traps" for him as minister.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) On 22 July, Roth told the king that he rejected the position. The king did not formally recognize his refusal, so as not give the impression that the Germans rejected him, and the position remained vacant until Gigurtu's resignation.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) It was also rumored that the Hungarian government was dissatisfied with Roth's appointment because Roth was German, whereas they thought the Hungarian minority was much bigger.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-32) In September 1940, [Ion Antonescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Antonescu "Ion Antonescu") was appointed Prime Minister, and on 8 September he asked Roth to join [his cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Antonescu_cabinet "Second Antonescu cabinet") as Minister of Justice. Ross refused, so Antonescu then offered him the Ministry of Education and eventually a ministry of his choice.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) Roth explained that his refusal was in objection to [Horia Sima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horia_Sima "Horia Sima") and his legionnaires from the Iron Guard still being in alliance with Antonescu.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30)

In 1943, by which time Schmidt had become head of the German Party, his conflict with Roth had a sudden climax when Roth opposed the enrollment of Romanian-Germans in the [Waffen SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waffen_SS "Waffen SS"), including Roth's son, with Schmidt responding on 28 September by calling him a public enemy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) Roth was accused of being a "traitor to the people" in December 1943 and was expelled from the now-named German Ethnic Group in Romania (the renamed German Party).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-33) Schmidt justified this further by saying that Roth was one of the rare exceptions that did not understand the Nazi revolution, and he added that this revealed his attitude toward the ethnic group.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) He also called Herbert Roth, Hans's son, a "slacker" and "coward" for refusing to join the Waffen-SS, so Hans challenged Schmidt to a duel. Schmidt refused, and Hans filed a defamation lawsuit which ended with a fine on Schmidt after the end of the war.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) Roth was also in contact with many members of the [German resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_resistance_to_Nazism "German resistance to Nazism") and the [Romanian resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_resistance_movement_during_World_War_II "Romanian resistance movement during World War II"), including [Hans Bernd von Haeften](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Bernd_von_Haeften "Hans Bernd von Haeften"), [Carl Friedrich Goerdeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Goerdeler "Carl Friedrich Goerdeler"), and [Ulrich von Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulrich_von_Hassell "Ulrich von Hassell"), all of whom were executed for their roles in [20 July plot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_July_plot "20 July plot"), and the communists [Vasile Luca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasile_Luca "Vasile Luca") and [Constantin Pîrvulescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_P%C3%AErvulescu "Constantin Pîrvulescu").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-cia-34) In July 1946, Roth wrote to Haeftens' widow, calling the plot a good act, as it bore positive fruit for Romanian-Germans as Germans would otherwise suffer.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30)

### Coup d'état and subsequent memorandums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Coup d'état and subsequent memorandums")]

On 23 August 1944, the day of [the Romanian coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Romanian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "1944 Romanian coup d'état"), Roth asked the Saxons and Swabians to be loyal to the Romanian state in order to avoid the stigmatization of the German minorities.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-pars-27) Then, in September, Roth urged Romanian-Germans not to flee the country and called for loyalty to the state of Romania, especially since many Swabians were leaving after the Nazi "Swabian Self-Protection" organization intimidated and frightened Swabians to evacuate [Banat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banat "Banat").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coup-35) On 27 October, Roth signed a memorandum which argued there was danger in punishing all Romanian-German supporters of Hitler, saying people who were not guilty were dragged, and he added that "the seducers and the seduced will be judged by the same measure".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coup-35) A few days later, on 31 October, Roth submitted another memorandum asking for the peaceful transfer of Protestant denominational schools to the German minority, explaining that the Nazis annexed the evangelical church through forceful means.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coup-35) He issued his final memorandum on 1 November, saying that innocent people were paying the price for the "disastrous policies of the former leaders", and asked Romanians to look at the long historical coexistence of Romanians and Romanian-Germans.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coup-35)

Through the Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession, Roth tried to establish an informal Saxon representation and inform Saxons about the situation in Romania in 1948.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-1948a-36) Writing in 1948, Roth blamed the SS actions of 1943, which conscripted ethnic Germans into military service with the approval of the Romanian government, calling it the "the most serious mistake in Saxon history".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-1948a-36) He feared that any association between the Saxons and paramilitary activity would lead to further reprisals against the Saxons that still lived in Romania, who are already lost their farmland as punishment for the 1943 SS conscriptions, so he asked West Germany to help prevent this.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-1948a-36)

[![Image 5: The Black Church of Brasov, Romania stands out in the foreground with a tree-covered mountain in the background, with the buildings of the city of Brasov dotting the foreground](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Biserica_Neagr%C4%83_%2848729880193%29.jpg/250px-Biserica_Neagr%C4%83_%2848729880193%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Biserica_Neagr%C4%83_(48729880193).jpg)

Roth's memorial service was held at the Black Church (pictured here) by the pastor Konrad Möckel.

The [Securitate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securitate "Securitate"), the Romanian intelligence agency, had made reports about Roth's anti-Nazi views with his activities in the German ethnic group in Romania after the coup, but ignored his attempts to distance himself from the Nazi movement as he was a former bourgeois politician.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) Roth was arrested for the first time in August 1948 by the [Siguranța](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siguran%C8%9Ba "Siguranța") while on vacation in [Sibiu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibiu "Sibiu").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-cia-34) He was accused by authorities of concealing his part ownership of a large Saxon bank owned by the Reich, which triggered a wave of alarm by the Saxons as they feared a new wave of persecution.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-cia-34) Roth was held for about eight weeks in the [Interior Ministry Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_Ministry_Palace "Interior Ministry Palace") in Bucharest before being released.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-read-30) During this time, a short trial was held about the case, where he was originally sentenced to 6 months in prison, but after appealing the verdict the case was dismissed.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-st-38)

In 1950, the house in which the Roth family resided on Constantin Noica Street in Sibiu, Romania, was expropriated.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) He moved to a house with other residents on Negruzzi Street, and took accounting courses to secure an income because he was forbidden from practicing law, his original occupation.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-st-38) He could not find a job, and so he did odd jobs with the support of his former friends.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) In February 1952, [Gavrilă Birtaș](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gavril%C4%83_Birta%C8%99&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gavrilă Birtaș (page does not exist)")([ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavril%C4%83_Birta%C8%99 "ro:Gavrilă Birtaș")), the head of the Securitate's Directorate of Domestic Surveillance, requested a file from the Securitate's Sibiu Regional Office.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) The report ended with the proposal to arrest Roth because of his influence among Germans in Romania, which was approved by Birtaș.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) Roth was arrested again on 15 April 1952 and labeled an "enemy of the people".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-kulturs-16) Numerous acquantinces of Roth's were then interrogated by the Securitate about Roth and Nazism, including Otto Herzog and Richard Zintz.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-39) The other prominent member of the German Party, Rudolf Brandsch, was arrested in Sibiu the night before.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37)

On 5 July 1952, the decision was made for Roth to go to administrative detention for 24 months, and he was ordered to be sent to the transit center in Bucharest on 21 July.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) He arrived at the transit center on 2 August 1952, and was then transported to [Bărăgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%83r%C4%83gan "Bărăgan") at a labor camp.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-de-37) According to testimonies from other prisoners, the labor camp in Bărăgan was shut down after Roth's family last visited in March, and he was then moved to Ghencea concentration camp.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-st-38) On 1 April 1953, Roth died in the Ghencea concentration camp, a camp for political prisoners in Bucharest.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-tradition-6) His family was not informed of his death.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-kulturs-16) His death certificate stated his cause of death was [uremia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uremia "Uremia").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-st-38) Roth's family disagreed with this and testified that they were never told exactly how he died.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-st-38) In May 1953, the protestant pastor of [Brașov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bra%C8%99ov "Brașov"), Konrad Möckel, held a memorial service at the [Black Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biserica_Neagr%C4%83 "Biserica Neagră") for Roth's family to commemorate his death.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-selb-25) Möckel spoke of Roth's devotion to the Saxons extensively.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-selb-25)

Religious leadership in the Evangelical Church
----------------------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Religious leadership in the Evangelical Church")]

From 1932 to 1949, Roth was regional church curator of the [Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession in Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Church_of_the_Augsburg_Confession_in_Romania "Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession in Romania").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-churchs-40) The regional church curator was the highest secular office in the church community, which supported the bishop in his duties and represented the bishop.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-nz-29)

### Leadership during Nazi control

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Leadership during Nazi control")]

In July 1941, Nazi-loyalty [Wilhelm Staedel](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wilhelm_Staedel&action=edit&redlink=1 "Wilhelm Staedel (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Staedel "de:Wilhelm Staedel")) was elected Bishop of the church with 60 of 105 votes, replacing [Viktor Glondys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Glondys "Viktor Glondys").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-42) The Nazi-controlled church leadership then attempted to transfer church assets and place church schools under the Nazi-controlled consistory.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41) Roth responded by advocating for a postponement, stating he had only just learned of the proposal and raised legal concerns such as the Volksgruppe not yet being constituted as a legal entity.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41) While he endorsed the principle of a transfer in general, he voted against Staedel's specific proposal, which was regardless approved a vote fo 12 to 6.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41) He changed his mind in 1942 and said the provisions of the proposal for the transfer that was adopted the previous year for not taking into account the church order's provisions, though he indicated his willingness to compromise by supporting amendments to the church order rather than rejecting the agreement entirely.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41) The Nazis eventually prevailed, achieving what historians have termed "self-Nazification" of the church through the explicit coordination between the Volksgruppe and Nazi-aligned church members.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41) Historians have attributed this outcome in part to a miscalculation by Glondys and/or Roth, who underestimated the extent of Nazi pressure and internal support for the movement within the church.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-coord-41) Roth asked for a resignation from the position of curator in March 1943, which he eventually withdrew after the [1944 Romanian coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Romanian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat "1944 Romanian coup d'état").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-churchs-40) In early 1944, in an audience with Minister of Culture [Ghiță Popp](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghi%C8%9B%C4%83_Popp&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghiță Popp (page does not exist)")([ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghi%C8%9B%C4%83_Popp "ro:Ghiță Popp")), Rudolf Brandsch said that Roth had illegally and without the approval of the Lutherans in Romania, placed himself as head of the Lutheran office in Hermannstadt.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-acc-43)

### Post Nazi-control period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Post Nazi-control period")]

In October 1944, Bishop [Wilhelm Staedel](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wilhelm_Staedel&action=edit&redlink=1 "Wilhelm Staedel (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Staedel "de:Wilhelm Staedel")) resigned, and Roth wished to replace Staedel as bishop with [episcopal vicar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_vicar "Episcopal vicar") Friedrich Müller, which Glondys disagreed with.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-muller-44) An agreement was made soon after where Roth took over the political contacts of the church with the government where he had to legitimize the newly [denazified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denazified "Denazified") church.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-muller-44) In January 1945, Glondys's claim to be bishop was rejected, which allowed for Müller to be elected, although he ran into some opposition initially due to his initial praise of Hitler in 1941 for being [anti-communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-communist "Anti-communist").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-muller-44) Friedrich Müller was elected bishop in 1945, and Roth was re-elected as curator until 31 March 1951.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-churchs-40) Roth was eliminated as regional church trustee in 1948 as a result of the "Sparkasse Trial", which concerned his former role as President of a Saxon savings bank.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-acc-43) Despite being acquitted, he chose not to run again in the 1949 church elections, presumably recognizing that his status as a former "bourgeois" parliamentarian made him a target for accusations that could effect Romanian Germans.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-acc-43) He had been on a leave of absence since October 1948.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-churchs-40)

Roles in Transylvanian Saxon institutions
-----------------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Otto_Roth&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Roles in Transylvanian Saxon institutions")]

In addition to his political career, Roth held numerous chairmanships in Transylvanian Saxons' institutions. He was the temporary president of the _Hermannstädter Allgemeine Sparkasse_, a credit bank, from 1928 to 1932, lending him influence in the economic field. Roth was also Chairman of the Sibiu Electricity Works from 1939 to 1942, alongside being Chairman of the Transylvanian German Publishing House.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-45)

Roth married Paula Copony in 1918.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-46) His father-in-law, Deputy Traugott Copony, held a seat in the [Hungarian Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Parliament "Hungarian Parliament"), and was close to the Romanian government.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-48) Together, Roth and Paula had a daughter, physicist [Marie Luise Roth-Höppner](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Luise_Roth-H%C3%B6ppner&action=edit&redlink=1 "Marie Luise Roth-Höppner (page does not exist)")([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Luise_Roth-H%C3%B6ppner "de:Marie Luise Roth-Höppner")), who was born in 1930 and made her residence in [Sibiu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibiu "Sibiu").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-child-49) They also had one son, Herbert Hoth, who like Maria Luise was sent to multiple correctional prisons starting in 1958 for possessing a letter written be detainee Fritz Theil.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-child-49)

In 2010, a commemorative plaque was unveiled at Roth's birthplace at Strada Tache Ionescu.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-str-3) In 2022, a film was shown in Sibiu about the life and work of Roth.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-50) He was also included in a special exhibition at the History Museum in Sighişoara on the law and constitutional practices of the Transylvanian Saxons, which the Department for Interethnic Relations presented in 2024.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-51) Thomas Frühmesser also wrote a [doctorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorate "Doctorate") on him in 2011.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Otto_Roth#cite_note-52)

Siebenbürgischer Homo politicus: Hans Otto Roth
===============================================

Das Institut für deutsche Kultur und Geschichte Südosteuropas an der LMU München (IKGS) lud am 18. November 2011 zu einem Vortragsabend über den siebenbürgischen Politiker Hans Otto Roth (1890-1953) in das Münchner Internationale Begegnungszentrum der Wissenschaft. 

Nach der Begrüßung durch den Direktor des IKGS, Prof. h.c. Dr. Stefan Sienerth, führte dessen Stellvertreter, Dr. Gerald Volkmer, in das Thema der Veranstaltung ein. Bereits der kurze Abriss der wichtigsten Ämter Dr. Hans Otto Roths zeichnete das Bild eines in den unterschiedlichsten gesellschaftlichen Bereichen engagierten Mannes. Sein Wirken als Rechtsanwalt, Journalist, führender politischer Vertreter der Siebenbürger Sachsen, Parlamentarier in beiden Bukarester Kammern, Landeskirchenkurator der Evangelischen Kirche A.B. in Rumänien und Präsident der Hermannstädter Allgemeinen Sparkassa zeigt die große Verantwortung, die Hans Otto Roth für die deutsche Minderheit in Siebenbürgen nach dem Ersten Weltkrieg zu tragen bereit war.

 Einen Überblick über die politischen Rahmenbedingungen zur Zeit Hans Otto Roths gab Florian Kührer. Der Doktorand, der sich auch in seiner Dissertation mit der Integration Siebenbürgens in den rumänischen Staat nach 1918 auseinandersetzt, forscht im Rahmen des Initiativkollegs „Europäische historische Diktatur- und Transformationsforschung“ an der Universität Wien. Er sprach über „Minderheit und Nationalstaat – die politischen Eliten Siebenbürgens und der Bukarester Zentralismus 1918–1940“. Damit steckte er die historischen und politischen Eckpunkte ab, die nötig waren, um das Wirken Hans Otto Roths im Kontext wechselnder politischer Systeme zu verstehen.![Image 7: Hans-Otto-Roth-Experten unter sich: Florian ...](https://www.siebenbuerger.de/bild/artikel/normal/2011/hansottoroth_2sp.jpg)

Hans-Otto-Roth-Experten unter sich: Florian Kührer, Dr. Florian Roth und Dr. Thomas Frühmesser (von links) bei der Abschlussdiskussion des Vortragsabends. Foto: Konrad Klein

 Speziell auf die Person Hans Otto Roths ging Thomas Frühmesser M.A. (Landau) ein, der Ende November mit einer Dissertation über den siebenbürgischen Politiker an der Universität Würzburg promoviert wurde. Seine Arbeit setzt sich mit der Rolle Hans Otto Roths in den politischen Strukturen der Siebenbürger Sachsen, seiner parlamentarischen Tätigkeit in Bukarest, seinen Funktionen in verschiedenen europäischen Minderheitengremien und insbesondere mit der Haltung Hans Otto Roths gegenüber dem Nationalsozialismus auseinander. In seinem Vortrag „Behauptungsversuche Hans Otto Roths als Minderheitenpolitiker gegenüber Nationalismus und Diktatur“ erläuterte der Referent die Positionen Hans Otto Roths gegenüber den verschiedenen politischen Systemen Rumäniens sowie seine Strategien zur Vertretung der Interessen der Rumäniendeutschen.

 In seinem Referat bewertete Dr. Florian Roth, Philosoph, Politologe und Münchner Stadtrat, der als Enkel Hans Otto Roths auch eine persönliche Verbindung zur Hauptperson des Abends besitzt, aus der Sicht eines Politikwissenschaftlers „Hans Otto Roths vielfältiges öffentliches Engagement und die Aktualität seiner politischen Position“. Kennzeichnend für die Politik Hans Otto Roths war sein Bestreben, auch unter wechselnden politischen Systemen eine angemessene Vertretung der deutschen Minderheit in Politik und Verwaltung zu erreichen, basierend auf seinem Credo „Volkstreue und Staatstreue“. Loyalität gegenüber dem Staat und Eintreten für die Rechte der eigenen Volksgruppe schlossen sich für Hans Otto Roth, der 1953 in einem stalinistischen Arbeitslager starb, nicht gegenseitig aus.

 Im Rahmen einer von Dr. Gerald Volkmer moderierten Abschlussdiskussion stellten sich die Referenten gemeinsam den Fragen des Publikums. Trotz gewisser Unterschiede in der Bewertung der politischen Zwänge, die auf Hans Otto Roth vor allem nach 1940 wirkten, würdigte das Plenum die Prinzipientreue eines Demokraten, der auch unter den Bedingungen zweier totalitärer Diktaturen das Wohl seiner Gemeinschaft über das eigene stellte.

The Hans Otto Roth Collection includes documents gathered in the period 1919–1951 by the creator of the collection in order to illustrate his activity as a political leader and journalist of the Transylvanian Saxons who opposed both the pre-communist extreme right movements and regimes and the communist regime.

### Name der Sammlung

### Sammlungsgeschichte und kulturelle Aktivitäten

*   The Hans Otto Roth Collection was created between 1919 and 1951, when its creator was one of the most important political leaders and journalists of the German minority in Romania. The documents which make up this collection were collected and organised according to the priorities of Hans Otto Roth’s political and journalistic activity. The documents are organised along two principles: chronological and thematic. From a thematic point of view,… [weiterlesen](http://cultural-opposition.eu/courage/individual/n25127?de#) The Hans Otto Roth Collection was created between 1919 and 1951, when its creator was one of the most important political leaders and journalists of the German minority in Romania. The documents which make up this collection were collected and organised according to the priorities of Hans Otto Roth’s political and journalistic activity. The documents are organised along two principles: chronological and thematic. From a thematic point of view, the documents are structured according to Roth’s most significant actions, such as his struggle against the takeover of the denominational schools of the Evangelical Church of Augustan Confession of Romania by the German Ethnic Group (an organisation controlled by the local Nazi movement), or his opposition in 1945–1948 to the implementation of abusive legislation concerning the German minority in Romania. It is interesting to note that the Roth Collection includes numerous duplicates of documents. This suggests that its creator had a double purpose in his mind: on the one hand, to bring his opposition to certain abusive measures to the attention of as many decision makers as possible, and, on the other hand, to preserve at least some copies of documents recording his actions.

The chronological limits of the documents in the Roth Collection reflect the period of his public activity. The year 1919 marks the beginning of Roth’s activity as deputy in the Romanian Parliament representing the German minority. The last year of Roth’s public activity may be considered to be 1951, because in 1952 he was arrested by Securitate. It is not known how the Hans Otto Roth Collection was saved after his arrest and imprisonment or how it became part of the Archives of the Honterus Parish Community, today known as the Black Church Archives and Library after the popular name of this historical parish church. The fact that Roth had several residences in different cities (Brașov, Sibiu, and Bucharest) accounts for the failure of the Securitate to confiscate all his documents. While those found at his work residence in Bucharest were seized by the secret police on the occasion of his arrest, the others could be at least partially preserved. According to Thomas Șindilariu, one of Roth’s acquaintances must have taken these documents and deposited them in a location owned by the Evangelical Church of Augustan Confession of Romania. However, there is no historical evidence regarding what happened to the Roth Collection between his arrest in 1952 and its official registration in 1962 in the recently established Archives of the Honterus Community. This institution was organised in accordance with the law of 1957 that allowed the creation of denominational archives. In 1958, the documents in the possession of the Honterus Parish Community were taken over by the Archives of the Community, and administered under the direct supervision of Gustav Markus, a former owner of the local Corvinus Publishing House and a person very familiar with the cultural heritage of the Transylvanian Saxons. Markus played a crucial role in preserving Roth’s documents and including them among the records of the newly established denominational archives. The Hans Otto Roth Collection was registered and archived in 1962, which meant that from this year onwards the collection was officially in the possession of this institution. The preservation of this collection represents an example of a silent but resolute resistance to the communist regime, which involved risks, as its creator Hans Otto Roth was perceived as an enemy of the regime. The Roth Collection remained in the possession of the denominational archives even after 1971, when the communist authorities issued Decree 472 regulating the transfer of church archives of historical value to the State Archives.

According to this decree, only documents concerning the current activity of the church were to remain in the possession of the denominational archives (Şindilariu 2005, 50–52). Thus, in 1974, after losing a large number of important historical documents, the Archives of the Honterus Community became an institution dedicated to serving the administrative activity of the local parish of the Evangelical Church. The Hans Otto Roth Collection had not been nationalised by the communist authorities, partly because of the ignorance of the employees of the State Archives in charge of selecting the collections to be transferred, and partly because Roth’s position as general curator of the Evangelical Church between 1932 and 1944 could have justified the keeping of his documents in the Archives of the Honterus Community. Since 1989, several Romanian and German scholars have carried out research in this collection, and in 2003 Klaus Popa edited a volume of documents concerning Hans Otto Roth’s activity between 1919 and 1951 on the basis of the records found in the custody of the Archives of the Honterus Community, also known as the Black Church Archives and Library (Popa 2003).

### Inhaltsbeschreibung

*   The Hans Otto Roth Collection includes four boxes of handwritten or printed documents, which reflect the activity of its creator as a political leader and journalist of the German community in Romania. Most of the documents are authored by Hans Otto Roth himself and represent memoranda sent to the Romanian state authorities in order to draw their attention to various abuses against the German minority, correspondence with personalities of the… [weiterlesen](http://cultural-opposition.eu/courage/individual/n25127?de#) The Hans Otto Roth Collection includes four boxes of handwritten or printed documents, which reflect the activity of its creator as a political leader and journalist of the German community in Romania. Most of the documents are authored by Hans Otto Roth himself and represent memoranda sent to the Romanian state authorities in order to draw their attention to various abuses against the German minority, correspondence with personalities of the time, articles for German-language newspapers in Romania, reports written as general curator of the Evangelical Church of Augustan Confession of Romania, and excerpts from the press.

These documents deal with very diverse topics: the Nazification of the German community in Romania and the opposition to the increased influence of Nazi ideas and organisations on the Romanian Germans; the deportation of Germans from Romania to the USSR in 1945; the nationalisations which affected the Romanian Germans in the period 1945–1948; and the internal struggles within the Evangelical Church for the election of a new bishop in 1945.

Hans Otto Roth
==============

 posted in: [„Das Meer der Bitterkeit“](https://www.memorialsighet.ro/category/de/gedenkstatte/das-meer-der-bitterkeit/) | 

(29 aprilie 1890, Sighişoara – 1 aprilie 1953, Ghencea)

![Image 8](https://www.memorialsighet.ro/hans-otto-roth-4/images/stories/hans%20otto%20roth.jpg)

avocat şi membru în Parlamentul României

studii de drept la Budapesta, Viena, Berlin si Zurich

Din 1917, activitati politice. Dupa Unire, s-a ocupat de integrarea minoritatii germane in Romania Mare, iar intre 1919 si 1938 a fost deputat si senator in parlamentul din Bucuresti

Orientat impotriva national-socialismului german, a protestat in 1933 la cancelarul Adolf Hitler contra prigonirii evreilor. Din 1935 pana in 1948 a fost avocat in Bucuresti si editor la ziarul Siebenburgisch-Deutschen Tageblattes, (Ziarul German din Translivania), cea mai importanta publicatie germana din Europa de Sud-Est.

Dupa intrarea Armatei Rosii in Romania in 1944, a incercat impreuna cu Rudolf Brandsch sa elaboreze un statut al drepturilor minoritatii germane. 

In 1948 a fost arestat si apoi eliberat dupa 6 luni. La 15 aprilie 1952, a fost arestat din nou de Securitatea din Brasov, atunci Orasul Stalin.A primit o condamnare administrativă de 24 luni, motivul încarcerării, menţionat în fişa de detenţie, fiind „fost deputat şi senator”. A fost închis în coloniile de muncă de la Fundulea şi Ghencea, precum şi în închisoarea-spital Văcăreşti.

A murit la 1 aprilie 1953, in lagarul Ghencea.Familia a aflat de moartea sa printr-o cunoştinţă care lucra la starea civilă, de la aceeaşi persoană având şi informaţia că e îngropat în cimitirul Ghencea, fără a li se indica locul exact.

Marie Luise Roth-Höppner (fiica lui Hans Otto Roth, condamnată și ea politic în lotul Bisericii Negre la 6 ani de închisoare) povesteşte despre circumstanțele în care ea și fratele ei Herbert au aflat despre decesul tatălui:

_Atunci frate-meu a umblat, săracul, peste tot. S-a dus întâi la pușcărie. (…) De acolo, de la poartă l-au gonit: „Ce vrei să știi?” Și, pe urmă a avut fratele meu o prietenă care iar a avut o prietenă care lucra la starea civilă și care a zis: „Să nu cumva să afle cineva că eu ți-am arătat certificatul de deces”. (…) Și atunci a știut frate-meu și a venit și ne-a înștiințat și pe noi. Și asta nu știu dacă a fost în aprilie-mai, dar a murit la 1 aprilie 1953 (…) la Ghencea… Acolo a fost și înmormântat. (…) Și s-a dus frate-meu – și m-am dus și eu odată cu el – s-a dus acolo, în satul Ghencea. Și acolo e în cimitir, din ce știa el, că doar n-o fi pus numele… Și atunci s-a dus la preotul de acolo, căruia îi era frică, bineînțeles. Și l-a convins și i-a zis… preotul a zis: „Stați aici, eu mă duc și acolo unde mă opresc, acolo este”. Și atunci s-a dus preotul acolo, apoi a plecat. Și frate-meu s-a dus în locul acela, numai că acolo erau mesteceni… Nici nu era loc de o groapă sau ceva. Frate-meu a făcut o cruce mică din lemn și a băgat-o acolo._

Fragment din interviul nr. 2878 cu Marie Luise Roth-Höppner, realizat de Andreea Cârstea, Sibiu, 9 decembrie 2009, Arhiva de istorie orală a Memorialului Victimelor Comunismului şi al Rezistenţei

**ROTH Hans Otto**, n. 29 apr. 1890, Sighişoara (Mureş), avocat, reprezentant al saşilor în Parlamentul României Mari; ar. 15 apr. 1952, cond. adm. 24 luni; † 1 apr. 1953, Ghencea (CI; Mem19; EŞ; AS2; FP; ASRI; RSC Bucureşti; DD) din _Cartea Morţilor_, Romulus Rusan (coord. şi studiu introductiv), Fundaţia Academia Civică, 2013

17.title: Otto Roth
17.content:
| Dr. Otto Roth |
| --- |
| [![Image 1: Dr. Otto Roth, a lawyer from Timisoara, is featured in a vintage black and white portrait](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Dr._Otto_Roth.jpg/250px-Dr._Otto_Roth.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dr._Otto_Roth.jpg) Portrait photograph, c. 1930 |
|  |
| Commissioner-in-Chief of the [Banat Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banat_Republic "Banat Republic") |
| **In office** 31 October 1918– 17 January 1919 |
| Preceded by | György Kórossy (as _[Alispán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isp%C3%A1n "Ispán")_) |
| Succeeded by | [Martin Filipon](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Filipon&action=edit&redlink=1 "Martin Filipon (page does not exist)") (as _[Župan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%BDupan "Župan")_) |
| Personal details |
| Born | December 6, 1884 [Nagy-Mutnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Daicoviciu,_Cara%C8%99-Severin "Constantin Daicoviciu, Caraș-Severin"), [Transleithania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lands_of_the_Crown_of_Saint_Stephen "Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen"), [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") |
| Died | April 22, 1956 (aged 71) [Timișoara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timi%C8%99oara "Timișoara"), [Romanian People's Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Romania "Socialist Republic of Romania") |
| Nationality | Hungarian Romanian Banatian |
| [Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party "Political party") | [Social Democratic Party of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_of_Hungary "Social Democratic Party of Hungary") |
| Other political affiliations | [Romanian Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Social_Democratic_Party_(1927%E2%80%9348) "Romanian Social Democratic Party (1927–48)") |
| Spouse | Rozalia Singer |
| Children | 3 |
| [Alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater "Alma mater") | [Eötvös Loránd University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E%C3%B6tv%C3%B6s_Lor%C3%A1nd_University "Eötvös Loránd University") [Leipzig University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig_University "Leipzig University") [Franz Joseph University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Joseph_University "Franz Joseph University") |
| Occupation | Lawyer, journalist, trade unionist, civil servant |
| Nickname | R. Otto Lippai |
|  |

**Otto Roth**, occasionally rendered as **Willy Otto Roth**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-snarget-1) or **Dr. Rot**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-Temperley_&_Otte,_p._347-2) ([Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language"): _Róth Ottó_; 6 December 1884 – 22 April 1956), was a Hungarian and Romanian lawyer, journalist and politician who served as the only Commissioner-in-Chief of the [Banat Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banat_Republic "Banat Republic"), between October 1918 and January 1919. Born a subject of the [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary"), [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Hungary "History of the Jews in Hungary") but non-religious, he was thirteen when he debuted as a literary journalist and magazine editor, with _Viribus Unitis_. In his twenties, he put out publications and founded literary circles, frequenting [Endre Ady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endre_Ady "Endre Ady"), [Gyula Juhász](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyula_Juh%C3%A1sz_(poet) "Gyula Juhász (poet)"), and [Zoltán Franyó](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Zolt%C3%A1n_Frany%C3%B3&action=edit&redlink=1 "Zoltán Franyó (page does not exist)"). Roth entered politics with the [Hungarian Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_of_Hungary "Social Democratic Party of Hungary") (MSZDP), and was a local councilor in [Timișoara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timi%C8%99oara "Timișoara") during most of World War I, emerging as a regional leader of the MSZDP before and during the [Aster Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aster_Revolution "Aster Revolution").

Roth is credited with proclaiming the Banat Republic on 31 October 1918—though the initiative was also attributed to [Albert Bartha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Bartha "Albert Bartha"), who briefly served as its military leader. The state was an autonomous extension of the [Hungarian Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Hungarian_Republic "First Hungarian Republic"), set up in order to prevent invasion by the [French Danube Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm%C3%A9e_d%27Orient_(1915%E2%80%9319) "Armée d'Orient (1915–19)"), but also aiming to preserve regional integrity against rival nationalisms. It was generally rejected by [Romanians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanians "Romanians") and [Serbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbs "Serbs"), who organized their own representative institutions. Unlike Bartha, Roth acknowledged the terms of the [Hungarian armistice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_Villa_Giusti "Armistice of Villa Giusti"), and was subsequently allowed to maintain his executive position by the [Kingdom of Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Serbia "Kingdom of Serbia"), which occupied Timișoara in November. His post became largely symbolic, as the [Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia "Kingdom of Yugoslavia") (also referred to as Yugoslavia), proclaimed that December, actively pursued an [annexation of the Banat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banat,_Ba%C4%8Dka_and_Baranja "Banat, Bačka and Baranja"); the Commissioner's importance was revived once French forces intervened as peacekeepers. With [Swabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banat_Swabians "Banat Swabians") support, Roth made an attempt at consolidating his Republic, but was ultimately chased out by Yugoslav soldiers in February 1919. Attempting to prevent the Banat's partition between Yugoslavia and the [Kingdom of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Romania "Kingdom of Romania"), he formed alliances with the French and the [Hungarian Soviet Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Soviet_Republic "Hungarian Soviet Republic") during the subsequent [Hungarian–Romanian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian%E2%80%93Romanian_War "Hungarian–Romanian War").

This episode ended with Roth's arrest by the [new conservative republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Republic_(1919%E2%80%931920) "Hungarian Republic (1919–1920)") in early 1920, though the [Hungarian Regency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1920%E2%80%931946) "Kingdom of Hungary (1920–1946)") cleared him of all charges, and released him. He was again imprisoned by Romanian troops, and released after promises to keep out of politics. He resumed his law practice in Timișoara, which remained on the Romanian side of the Banat partitions. His earlier activity was a subject of repeated criticism by [Romanian nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_nationalism "Romanian nationalism"), and became a topic of litigation. As reported by his friend Nicolae Brînzeu, Roth eventually went back on his pledge to remain apolitical; campaigning for Banat autonomy, he embraced "[anti-Bolshevik communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Stalinist_left "Anti-Stalinist left")" and [anti-fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-fascism "Anti-fascism"), and supported another friend, [Petru Groza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petru_Groza "Petru Groza"), who was emerging as an important figure on the Romanian far-left. During the early stages of World War II, politician [Constantin Argetoianu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Argetoianu "Constantin Argetoianu") employed Roth as his contact with the Romanian left-wing circles. According to Brînzeu, Roth also sought to prevent clashes between Romania and Regency Hungary, and especially the rapprochement between [Hungarian revisionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_revisionism "Hungarian revisionism") and [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany").

Defeated in this effort, Roth was also exposed to antisemitic persecution, and reportedly prepared himself and his Jewish community for [resettlement in Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar_Plan "Madagascar Plan"). He was publicly defended by Groza during World War II, and also networked to have Groza released from prison in 1944. Following the [King Michael Coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Michael_Coup "King Michael Coup"), he made a final return to politics, rallying with the [Romanian Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Social_Democratic_Party_(1927%E2%80%9348) "Romanian Social Democratic Party (1927–48)"). With Groza becoming [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Romania "Prime Minister of Romania"), Roth received minor roles in either government or state-owned business, and continued to be involved in cultural affairs. Brînzeu however notes that he remained staunchly critical of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") and the [Romanian Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Communist_Party "Romanian Communist Party"), objecting to Groza's close relationship with both. Brînzeu and Roth were placed under surveillance by the [Securitate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securitate "Securitate").

Otto Roth was born to a [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Hungary "History of the Jews in Hungary") family in Nagy-Mutnik, in the [Hungarian division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lands_of_the_Crown_of_Saint_Stephen "Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen") of [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") (now [Mâtnicu Mare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_Daicoviciu,_Cara%C8%99-Severin "Constantin Daicoviciu, Caraș-Severin"), Romania).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-gneum-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-bjy2006-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-adevarul-5) His father was Miksa Roth, a well-to-do local liquor merchant.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-bjy2006-4) Otto and Árpád Roth were the two sons born from his marriage to Helén Fischer (1853–1939).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-6) The Roths were "very distant" relatives of poet [Erik Majtényi](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Erik_Majt%C3%A9nyi&action=edit&redlink=1 "Erik Majtényi (page does not exist)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-majt%C3%A9nyi-7) By 1930, Otto was no longer an observant Jew, although he was not hostile to religion in general.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-gneum-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-adevarul-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-8) Various authors describe the German-speaking Roth as belonging to the [Swabian community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banat_Swabians "Banat Swabians").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-astwm-9) According to historian [Victor Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Neumann "Victor Neumann"), Roth did not reject [Zionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zionism "Zionism"), seeing it as compatible with the socialist platform, but only envisaged [emancipation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_emancipation "Jewish emancipation")—"an equality of rights was enough." In this, Roth was critical of [Jewish assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_assimilation "Jewish assimilation"), which had driven most of his correligionists to declare themselves Hungarian.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-V._Neumann,_p._16-10) Neumann also views Roth as representative for the "diversity of the Jews' condition": while some "struggle[d] for a social position and implicitly for equality of rights", Roth advanced into mainstream society to hold some "key positions".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-V._Neumann,_pp._15%E2%80%9316-11)

Young Roth was educated at Kun Calvinist High School (now Aurel Vlaicu Lyceum) in [Szászváros (Orăștie)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Or%C4%83%C8%99tie "Orăștie"), where he met and befriended Groza and the future [Greek Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Greek_Catholic_Church "Romanian Greek Catholic Church") priest Nicolae Brînzeu, who remained Roth's lifelong friends.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-gneum-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-bjy2006-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-adevarul-5)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-12) When their math teacher Aladár Tokaji hit a colleague on the head, Groza and Roth, already showing his "revolutionary tendencies", organized a student strike. All members of the class walked out of the school, finally obtaining Tokaji's removal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-gyermekkor-13) In 1897–1898, Roth, together with Brînzeu and another future politician, Nándor Hegedűs, edited a student magazine called _Viribus Unitis_ (Latin for "With United Forces").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-14) The expression, used as a motto by the [House of Habsburg-Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Habsburg-Lorraine "House of Habsburg-Lorraine"), "was intended as a symbol of the unity between young people of different nationalities."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-15) As noted by Groza, their class of 1903 was educated by adherents of [Liberal Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Christianity "Liberal Christianity"), giving students "opportunities to express our sense of belonging, regardless of race, religion, or nationality."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-gyermekkor-13)

According to Groza's recollections, Roth went on to graduate in Law and Economics from the [Budapest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E%C3%B6tv%C3%B6s_Lor%C3%A1nd_University "Eötvös Loránd University"), before furthering his studies in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and at the [Leipzig University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig_University "Leipzig University").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-bjy2006-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-adevarul-5) Poet Béla Serestély, who was himself a graduate of the Kun, recalls that Roth was a student in [Pest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pest,_Hungary "Pest, Hungary"); in 1903,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-egynap-16) together with another fellow graduate, András Jakab, and with Kázmér Konkoly Thege, he put out _Előre_ ("Forward"), a "university youth newspaper".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-irado-17) Serestély joined the writing staff, alongside philosophy students [Gyula Juhász](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyula_Juh%C3%A1sz_(poet) "Gyula Juhász (poet)") and [Béla Vágó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_V%C3%A1g%C3%B3 "Béla Vágó").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-irado-17) For this enterprise, Roth used the pen name _R. Otto Lippai_; other contributors included [Lux Terka](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lux_Terka&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lux Terka (page does not exist)"), [Renée Erdős](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9e_Erd%C5%91s "Renée Erdős") (with fragments of her short story "Kleopátra"), and the "proletarian poet" [Sándor Csizmadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A1ndor_Csizmadia "Sándor Csizmadia").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Roth#cite_note-egynap-16)
